stances.claim: The reaction was immediate -- and fierce: Rotarians were aghast, warning that religion had no place in a civic institution built on pluralism and neutrality; the credo was divisive, unprecedented, risky; some feared it would alienate non-Christian members, others worried it would reduce Rotary's work to moral exhibitionism. No one could recall a Rotary president anywhere who had framed his term so explicitly in theological language.

stances.claim: Art listened patiently, explained calmly, did not retreat -- he argued that Rotary's foundational maxims ('Service Above Self' + 'He Profits Most Who Serves Best') were not merely civic slogans but moral truths, deeply consonant with the commandment to love one's neighbor; his credo, he insisted, was not an imposition of belief but a clarification of purpose. Faith, for him, was not sectarian -- it was catalytic.

Skepticism followed him into the ballroom.

stances.claim: Then, four days later, the earth itself intervened -- on July 16, 1990 a 7.7-magnitude earthquake tore through Luzon, flattening communities, burying buildings, and killing more than 2,000 people; Baguio lay in ruins; panic spread faster than information; suffering arrived before response.

stances.claim: At the next Rotary meeting there was no prepared speech -- Art stood and made an appeal, not for ceremony, not for recognition, but for immediate action; he asked the Club to help the poor, the injured, the displaced. Within thirty minutes pledges reached ₱5.5 million; by the next day contributions exceeded expectations many times over; doctors volunteered, businessmen redirected resources, Rotary Anns mobilized clothing and food; a tent city rose in Burnham Park sheltering hundreds of families. Rotary clubs abroad responded as well -- the Rotary Club of Waikiki organized a massive airlift, over 3,300 kilograms of relief goods flown in from Hawaii.

stances.claim: This was not charity as gesture -- it was compassion as mobilization; standing amid the whirlwind of response, Art understood something fundamental about leadership: conviction, when aligned with compassion, could move institutions faster than policy, more decisively than procedure, and more enduringly than rhetoric. His credo had been tested -- not in theory but in catastrophe. And it had held.

one_paragraph_summary: Art's most-tested credo chapter -- the announcement at his Rotary Club of Manila inauguration on July 12, 1990 of a theological-language credo, 'LOVE GOD. SERVE MAN.,' that drew 'immediate and fierce' reaction from Rotarians who warned that religion had no place in a civic institution built on pluralism. He listened patiently, explained calmly, did not retreat -- arguing that Rotary's foundational maxims ('Service Above Self,' 'He Profits Most Who Serves Best') were 'not merely civic slogans but moral truths,' deeply consonant with the commandment to love one's neighbor, and that his credo was 'not an imposition of belief but a clarification of purpose.' At his inauguration he distributed a 76-page Program of Action unprecedented in the Club's history -- 178 projects, calendar of execution, ₱90 million budget. Four days later, on July 16, 1990, 'the earth itself intervened': a 7.7-magnitude earthquake tore through Luzon, killing over 2,000 people, leaving Baguio in ruins. At the next meeting there was 'no prepared speech' -- Art made an appeal for immediate action; 'within thirty minutes pledges reached ₱5.5 million,' a Burnham Park tent city rose sheltering hundreds of families, and the Rotary Club of Waikiki organized a 3,300-kilogram airlift from Hawaii. This was 'not charity as gesture -- it was compassion as mobilization.' The chapter's thesis: 'conviction, when aligned with compassion, could move institutions faster than policy, more decisively than procedure, and more enduringly than rhetoric. His credo had been tested -- not in theory, but in catastrophe. And it had held.' Closing: 'faith, when married to action, was not divisive at all. It was transformative.'
